claim: Weakly electric fish generate low-intensity electric fields to navigate and interact with conspecifics, even in complete darkness.
source: These fish, through their electric organ, generate low-intensity electric fields to navigate and interact with conspecifics, even in complete darkness.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known characteristic of weakly electric fish, drawing on established scientific knowledge about these organisms.

claim: Brown ghost knifefish possess a rich electric 'vocabulary' made by individually variable and sex-specific electric signals.
source: The brown ghost knifefish is appealing as a study subject due to a rich electric 'vocabulary', made by individually variable and sex-specific electric signals.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by the broader literature on brown ghost knifefish communication, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Electric signals in brown ghost knifefish are mainly characterized by brief frequency modulations of the oscillating dipole moment continuously generated by their electric organ, known as chirps.
source: These are mainly characterized by brief frequency modulations of the oscillating dipole moment continuously generated by their electric organ, and are known as chirps.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about chirps in brown ghost knifefish, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Different types of chirps are believed to convey specific and behaviorally salient information, serving as behavioral readouts for different internal states during behavioral observations.
source: Different types of chirps are believed to convey specific and behaviorally salient information, serving as behavioral readouts for different internal states during behavioral observations.
evidence: This represents the existing hypothesis in the field (communication-hypothesis) that the authors are challenging, based on prior literature.

claim: The code to decipher the electric communication of brown ghost knifefish remains unknown despite seven decades of neuroethological research.
source: Despite the success of this model in neuroethology over the past seven decades, the code to decipher their electric communication remains unknown.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field, representing a gap in understanding.

claim: Chirps function as specialized self-directed signals that enhance conspecific electrolocation during social encounters.
source: By uncovering correlations among chirping, electric field geometry, and detectability in enriched environments, we present evidence for a previously unexplored role of chirps as specialized self-directed signals, enhancing conspecific electrolocation during social encounters.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis and finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental approaches and data analyses presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Bats emit high-pitch calls (8–200 kHz) to detect features of stationary or moving objects while flying at high speeds and in complete darkness.
source: by emitting high-pitch calls (8–200 kHz; Fenton et al., 1998), bats are able to detect features of stationary or moving objects while flying at high speeds and in complete darkness (Jones and Holderied, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research on bat echolocation.

claim: Odontocete cetaceans are capable of echolocating objects by emitting very short clicks covering a broad frequency spectrum (5 Hz-100 kHz).
source: Similarly, odontocete cetaceans are capable of echolocating objects by emitting very short (a few ms long) clicks covering a broad frequency spectrum (5 Hz-100 kHz).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cetacean echolocation capabilities.

claim: A few other mammals (shrews and tenrecs), bird species (oilbirds and swiftlets) and even blind humans are capable of echolocating target objects through the emission of brief high-frequency echolocation calls.
source: A few other mammals (shrews and tenrecs), but also bird species (oilbirds and swiftlets) and even blind humans (Griffin, 1944; Thaler et al., 2011), are known to be capable of echolocating target objects through the emission of brief high-frequency echolocation calls (Konishi and Knudsen, 1979; Brinkløv et al., 2013; Gould, 1965).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research on echolocation in various species.

claim: Brown ghosts belong to the gymnotiform group and occupy benthic habitats in the Amazon river basin.
source: Brown ghosts belong to the gymnotiform group (as does the electric eel) and occupy benthic habitats in the Amazon river basin (Crampton, 2019).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the taxonomy and habitat of brown ghost knifefish, supported by a citation.

claim: Brown ghosts generate quasi-sinusoidal electric fields at relatively high frequencies (600–1000 Hz).
source: They generate quasi-sinusoidal electric fields at relatively high frequencies (600–1000 Hz; Zakon et al., 2002) by means of modified motor neurons projecting mainly to the caudal region of the fish body where they form a so-called electric organ.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research on brown ghost electric organ discharges.

claim: Passive electrolocation is possible only at shorter ranges (0–5 cm).
source: Compared to echolocation, passive electrolocation is possible only at shorter ranges (0–5 cm; Lissmann and Machin, 1958; von der Emde, 1999; Knudsen, 1974) and, although it is so fast to be considered almost instantaneous, it is more sensitive to signal degradation (Benda, 2020; Nelson and MacIver, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research on electrolocation ranges.

claim: Active electrolocation allows detection of surrounding objects up to 10–12 cm away from the skin.
source: Active electrolocation allows to extend the active space of electrolocation (Hopkins and Westby, 1986; Brenowitz, 1982) slightly beyond such short range: since EODs spread roughly equally in all directions, all affected surrounding objects (preys, substrate, vegetation) are simultaneously detected (up to 10–12 cm away from the skin; von der Emde, 1999; Snyder et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research on active electrolocation ranges.

claim: During social interactions, the range of active electrolocation can be extended to within a 30–40 cm radius through beat detection.
source: During social interactions, the range of active electrolocation can be further extended: when two fish approach each other, the alternating constructive and destructive interaction of their sinewave EODs results in an amplitude- and phase-modulated signal (also referred to as beat) detectable by each of them within a 30–40 cm radius (see appendix 1: Detecting beats at a distance; Knudsen, 1975; Fotowat et al., 2013; Henninger et al., 2018; Benda, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research on beat detection ranges.

claim: At 27 °C female brown ghost EOD frequencies range between 600 and 800 Hz while male frequencies are usually between 800 and 1000 Hz.
source: at 27 °C female EOD frequencies range between 600 and 800 Hz while male frequencies are usually between 800 and 1000 Hz.
evidence: This is established knowledge about sex differences in EOD frequencies in brown ghost knifefish.

claim: Low DFs may be indicative of same sex encounters, whereas high DFs could signal opposite sex interactions.
source: It follows that low DFs may be indicative of same sex encounters, whereas high DFs could signal opposite sex interactions (Bastian et al., 2001).
evidence: This is an inference based on the sex differences in EOD frequencies, supported by a citation.

claim: Weakly electric fish can passively detect bioelectric sources in close proximity to their body (0–5 cm).
source: In summary, weakly electric fish are capable of passively detecting bioelectric sources in close proximity to their body (0–5 cm), but also to actively sense inanimate objects as instantaneous EOD perturbations (up to 12 cm; Chen et al., 2005; Snyder et al., 2007; Fotowat et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research on electrolocation ranges.

claim: Weakly electric fish can actively sense inanimate objects as instantaneous EOD perturbations up to 12 cm.
source: In summary, weakly electric fish are capable of passively detecting bioelectric sources in close proximity to their body (0–5 cm), but also to actively sense inanimate objects as instantaneous EOD perturbations (up to 12 cm; Chen et al., 2005; Snyder et al., 2007; Fotowat et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research on active electrolocation.

claim: Weakly electric fish can instantaneously sense the presence of other conspecifics at distances of up to 30–50 cm by detecting beats.
source: In addition, by detecting beats (i.e. the EOD amplitude modulations induced by other EOD emitting sources), they can instantaneously sense the presence of other conspecifics at distances of up to 30–50 cm (Fotowat et al., 2013; Henninger et al., 2018; Silva A., personal communication).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research and personal communication.

claim: The strength of electric fields decays with the cubed distance.
source: Importantly, the strength of electric fields decays with the cubed distance (see appendix 1) and EODs are subject to anisotropic degradation even at very short ranges.
evidence: This is a statement about the physics of electric field propagation, representing established knowledge.

claim: EODs are subject to anisotropic degradation even at very short ranges, mainly due to the presence of noisy interferences encountered during locomotion through electrically heterogeneous underwater materials.
source: Importantly, the strength of electric fields decays with the cubed distance (see appendix 1) and EODs are subject to anisotropic degradation even at very short ranges. This is mainly due to the presence of noisy interferences encountered during locomotion through electrically heterogeneous underwater materials (Gómez-Sena et al., 2014; Pedraja et al., 2016; Milam et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research on EOD signal degradation.

claim: Chirps can be broadly classified in at least 4 different types, based on their duration and the extent of the chirp frequency modulation.
source: These consist of brief EOD frequency modulations – or chirps – which can be broadly classified in at least 4 different types, based on their duration and the extent of the chirp frequency modulation (FM, Engler et al., 2000; Zupanc et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research on chirp classification.

claim: Both chirps and positional parameters can only be detected as perturbations of the beat via the same electroreceptors.
source: Since both chirps and positional parameters (such as size, orientation, or motion) can only be detected as perturbations of the beat (Petzold et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2012; Fotowat et al., 2013), and via the same electroreceptors, the inputs relaying both types of information are likely to overlap and interact in highly variable ways (as noted also by Field et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research on beat processing and electroreception.

claim: The majority of chirps are produced within a short range (<50 cm).
source: Moreover, as the majority of chirps are produced within a short range (<50 cm; Zupanc et al., 2006; Hupé et al., 2008; Henninger et al., 2018; see appendix 1) this interference is likely to occur consistently during social interactions.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research on chirp production ranges.

claim: A total of 67,522 chirps were obtained from staged social pairings, playback experiments and behavioral assessments of fish locomotory activity.
source: We have gathered a large dataset of circa 67.000 chirps, obtained from staged social pairings, playback experiments and behavioral assessments of fish locomotory activity (see Table 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data collected in the study, as shown in Table 2.

claim: The relative number of different chirp types in a given recording does not significantly correlate with any particular behavioral or social context.
source: We first show that the relative number of different chirp types in a given recording does not significantly correlate with any particular behavioral or social context.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study, supported by the factor analysis and other statistical analyses presented in the results.

claim: The relative number of different chirp types is correlated to the biophysical properties of underwater electric fields and to the spatial arrangement of interacting EODs.
source: It is instead correlated to the biophysical properties of underwater electric fields and to the spatial arrangement of interacting EODs.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study, supported by the analyses of chirp interference and electric images.

claim: K-means chirp clustering indicated an optimal value of 2–3 for clustering chirps based on duration and frequency modulation parameters.
source: Through this approach, 2 clusters were identified (clustering was validated using the silhouette method; Rousseeuw, 1987), suggesting a roughly bimodal distribution of chirps, according to these basic features (a third cluster could be defined by the separation between type 1 and type 2 chirps, which in our sample was not so obvious).
evidence: This claim is supported by the k-means clustering analysis shown in Figure 1C and validated using the silhouette method.

claim: Chirps were categorized using cut-off values based on the distribution density: duration = 50ms, FM = 105 Hz.
source: Based on these cut-off values (duration = 50ms, FM = 105 Hz), chirps were categorized in short (with small - type 2 - or large - type 1 - FM) and long (with small - rises - or large - type 3 - FM; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about how chirps were classified in the study, shown in Figure 1.

claim: The majority of chirps were produced by male subjects.
source: Overall, the majority of chirps were produced by male subjects, at rates that seemed affected by environmental experience (resident, intruder or equal; Appendix 1—figure 2A, C), social status (dominant or subordinate; Appendix 1—figure 2B) and social experience (novel or experienced; Appendix 1—figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Appendix 1—figure 2.

claim: Sex differences in chirp production were reversed when fish were allowed to interact freely, as opposed to being separated by a plastic mesh divider.
source: Interestingly, this sex difference was reversed when fish were allowed to interact freely, as opposed to being separated by a plastic mesh divider (Appendix 1—figure 2E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Appendix 1—figure 2E, F.

claim: Sex differences were found in the types of chirp produced, mainly in the case of male-to-female exchanges.
source: Sex differences were found also in the types of chirp produced, mainly in the case of male-to-female exchanges (MF; Appendix 1—figure 2C, D), confirming previous accounts of marked sex dimorphisms in both the number and the type of chirps produced by brown ghosts (Dye, 1987; Zupanc and Maler, 1993; Dulka and Maler, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Appendix 1—figure 2C, D and citations to previous research.

claim: Tank experience, DF and context are the most important factors explaining chirp variance, accounting for 52.3% of the total variance.
source: The lowest number of variables required to explain the highest percentage of variance (N=3: tank experience, DF and context) was obtained by further simplifying the model through subsequent iterations (percent of variance explained 52.3%).
evidence: This claim is supported by the factor analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Environmental and social experience, together with beat frequency (DF) are the most important factors explaining chirp variability.
source: Overall, this analysis indicated that environmental and social experience, together with beat frequency (DF) are the most important factors explaining chirp variability (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the factor analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Chirp parameters such as duration and FM do not seem to be associated with any particular context in a meaningful way, other than being affected by beat frequency.
source: It also indicates that chirp parameters such as duration and FM do not seem to be associated with any particular context in a meaningful way, other than being affected by beat frequency.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the factor analysis results shown in Figure 2.

claim: Brown ghosts do not respond to playback chirps in a chirp-type specific manner.
source: Overall, these results show that brown ghosts do not respond to playback chirps in a chirp-type specific manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by the playback experiment results shown in Figure 3.

claim: Fish responses to plain sinewave EODs confirmed that fish respond with large chirps (type 1 and type 3) to high DFs and with small chirps (type 2) to low DF signals.
source: Fish responses to plain sinewave EODs confirmed previously reported findings: fish respond with large chirps (type 1 and type 3) to high DFs and with small chirps (type 2) to low DF signals (Appendix 1—figure 4), with males producing more chirps than females (Figure 3B; Bastian et al., 2001; Engler and Zupanc, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by the playback experiment data shown in Figure 3B and Appendix 1—figure 4, and citations to previous research.

claim: A transient decrease in chirping was observed in the immediate temporal surround of playback chirps.
source: Notably, a transient decrease in chirping was observed in the immediate temporal surround of playback chirps (modes 1–3, Appendix 1—figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Appendix 1—figure 5.

claim: The number of type 2 chirps seems to increase over time during playback trials.
source: Analysis of the time course of chirping further revealed two interesting details: first, while type 1 and type 3 chirps seem to be randomly scattered throughout the whole trial (60 s), the number of type 2 chirps seems to increase over time (Appendix 1—figure 6; as reported by Hupé et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Appendix 1—figure 6 and a citation to previous research.

claim: The vast majority of rises was produced right at the end of the playback signal, regardless of whether or not playback chirps were occurring.
source: Second, the vast majority of rises was produced right at the end of the playback signal, regardless of whether or not playback chirps were occurring (Appendix 1—figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Appendix 1—figure 6.

claim: The production of chirps and the detection of non self-generated chirps may be two independent processes.
source: Finally, these findings indicate that, irrespective of the meaning or valence chirps may have, the production of chirps and the detection of non self-generated chirps may be two independent processes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of chirp-type specific responses in the playback experiments.

claim: Chirps are produced at higher rates when playback frequency gets closer to the fish's own EOD frequency (i.e. reaching a low DF value).
source: Perhaps not surprisingly, we found that chirps are produced at higher rates when playback frequency gets closer to the fish's own EOD frequency (i.e. reaching a low DF value), similarly to what happens when static frequency playbacks are used.
evidence: This claim is supported by the frequency ramp playback experiment results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Each individual fish displayed rather similar chirping patterns, both across trials of different length as well as in repeats of the same trial.
source: Despite this heterogeneity, each individual fish displayed rather similar chirping patterns, both across trials of different length as well as in repeats of the same trial (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4D–F.

claim: The overall number of chirps was reliably correlated with trial duration with a linear correlation coefficient of R2=0.987.
source: In addition, regardless of the type of chirp produced in a given trial, the overall number of chirps was reliably correlated with trial duration with an astonishingly high linear correlation coefficient (R2=0.987, Appendix 1—figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Appendix 1—figure 7.

claim: Chirp type choice on average appears to reflect changes in the DF sign.
source: As previously shown, chirp type choice on average appears to reflect changes in the DF sign: larger chirps are scarcer around 0 Hz, while smaller ones are more frequent around the smaller DF values (Figure 4G–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4G–I.

claim: The reliability by which the chirping response adapts to both the rate and direction of beat frequency is variable across individuals but rather stable across trials.
source: The reliability by which the chirping response adapts to both the rate and direction of beat frequency is variable across individuals but rather stable across trials (relative to a given subject), further suggesting that chirp type variations may not reflect changes in internal states or in the animal motivation to specific behavioral displays (presumably subject to less abrupt variations and stereotypical patterning based on DF).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the frequency ramp playback experiment results, suggesting that chirp type choice is not related to internal states.

claim: Chirp patterning is mainly affected by beat frequency (i.e. DF).
source: Taken together, these results indicate that chirp patterning is mainly affected by beat frequency (i.e. DF).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the frequency ramp playback experiment results.

claim: Type 2 chirps are overall the most frequently produced chirp type, both in females as well as males.
source: Considering all recordings independently, type 2 chirps are overall the most frequently produced chirp type, both in females as well as males (Appendix 1—figure 3A, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Appendix 1—figure 3A, C.

claim: The most common chirp type transition found is 'type 2'-'type 2', except for the case in which males are chirping to females.
source: As a direct consequence, the most common chirp type transition found is 'type 2'-'type 2', except for the case in which males are chirping to females (labeled as MF; Appendix 1—figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the chirp transition analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 3B.

claim: At an individual level, the most common chirp sequence is a repeat of type 2 chirps in both males and females.
source: Overall, these results show that, at an individual level, the most common chirp sequence is a repeat of type 2 chirps in both males and females, with type composition being only slightly more heterogeneous for male senders, when paired with female receivers.
evidence: This is a summary of the chirp transition analysis results.

claim: Chirp-type patterning is highly conservative and not connected to any of the behavioral contexts considered, except the one identified by low vs high DFs.
source: In other words, at least when chirp sequences are considered individually, chirp-type patterning is highly conservative and not connected to any of the behavioral contexts considered, except the one identified by low vs high DFs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the chirp transition analysis.

claim: The temporal correlation of chirp series was highly variable among fish pairs.
source: In our recordings, although the temporal correlation of chirp series was highly variable among fish pairs (Figure 5), it often on the number of chirps produced (as shown also by estimates of the maximum chirp rates in Zupanc et al., 2006, chirp rate 0.4 /s; Hupé et al., 2008, chirp rate 0.53 /s; Henninger et al., 2018, chirp rate 3 /s) raising the question of whether the previously reported temporal correlations could be just a direct consequence of higher chirp rates occurring when fish get closer to each other (Zupanc et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 5 and citations to previous research.

claim: The most frequent chirp transitions were self-referenced (1–1 or 2–2).
source: What stood out most consistently from this analysis was the much lower (or sometimes completely absent) extent of sender-receiver chirp transitions, as shown by the higher transition probabilities along the 1–1 and 2–2 quadrants of the probability maps. According to this, cross-correlation indices are very low or near zero levels in all cases (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the chirp transition analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Cross-correlation would not be significantly affected during courtship.
source: Although female fish produced a surprisingly higher number of chirps in these conditions, only minimal signs of cross-correlation could be detected, without reaching on average the threshold for statistical significance (Figure 5J).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data from the breeding condition experiments shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Brown ghosts utilize a very limited variety of chirp type transitions in different behavioral contexts.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that brown ghosts utilize a very limited variety of chirp type transitions in different behavioral contexts and do not emit specific chirp patterns in any given behavioral context analyzed.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the chirp transition analysis across different behavioral contexts.

claim: Chirp time series produced by different fish during paired interactions are consistently independent of each other.
source: More importantly, they show that – at least in the social conditions analyzed here and within small-sized time windows – chirp time series produced by different fish during paired interactions are consistently independent of each other.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Chirps occurred often during active locomotion (directed either forward or backwards).
source: Chirps occurred often during active locomotion (directed either forward or backwards), type 3 chirps seemed to occur more evidently towards the end of a forward-oriented swimming bout, while rises appeared to be centered around forward locomotion (loc, Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the PSTH analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Chirps do not seem to trigger any defensive or aggressive behavior directly.
source: Although all chirp types were used during aggressive interactions, these seemed to be rather less frequent in the immediate surround of the chirps (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the PSTH analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Type 2 chirps are mostly produced in repeats and predominantly during backward swimming (knife).
source: This allowed us to make the following considerations: (1) as previously observed, type 2 chirps are the most represented chirp type. They are mostly produced in repeats and predominantly during backward swimming (knife), they are also followed – to a lower extent – by direct contact (wrestle), head bites (atk), backward tail-to-tail swimming (tail1), escape attempts (esc), type 3 chirps, head butts and chasing
evidence: This claim is supported by the transition matrix analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Chirps are produced more often during locomotion or scanning-related motor activity.
source: Overall, these results provided mutually reinforcing evidence indicating that chirps are produced more often during locomotion or scanning-related motor activity and confirm previous reports of a lower occurrence of chirping during more direct aggressive contact (as shown also by Triefenbach and Zakon, 2008; Hupé et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral analysis shown in Figure 6, supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Chirping may be linked more strongly with scanning and environmental exploration than with a particular motivational state.
source: The significantly higher extent of chirping during swimming and locomotion, consistently confirmed by four different approaches (PSTH, TM, CN, MDS), suggests that – although chirp-behavior correlations may exist at time-scales larger than those here considered – chirping may be linked more strongly with scanning and environmental exploration than with a particular motivational state, thus confirming findings from our playback experiments.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Emitted chirps were often localized in correspondence with areas of high beat interference.
source: By plotting both beat-interference values and chirp abundance by DF, we found that emitted chirps were indeed often localized in correspondence with areas of high interference: at negative DFs, chirps were localized mainly in the type 2 range, whereas at positive DFs recorded chirps overlapped more often with the type 1 and 3 ranges (Appendix 1—figure 9C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the beat interference analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 9C.

claim: A high degree of matching was found between the DF values at which the interference is higher and those at which chirps were actually recorded.
source: Eventually, by calculating the normalized cumulative interference for each chirp type, a high degree of matching was found between the DF values at which the interference is higher and those at which chirps were actually recorded (Appendix 1—figure 9B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the beat interference analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 9B.

claim: Type 2 chirps at low or even negative DFs may induce similar interference levels as those induced by larger chirps at higher beat frequencies.
source: A chirp type comparison (Appendix 1—figure 9D) further revealed that type 2 chirps at low or even negative DFs may induce similar interference levels as those induced by larger chirps at higher beat frequencies.
evidence: This claim is supported by the beat interference comparison shown in Appendix 1—figure 9D.

claim: Chirps consistently alter beats and EIs, at all the different reciprocal positions considered.
source: This indicates that chirps consistently alter beats and EIs, at all the different reciprocal positions considered, thus supporting the idea that chirp-triggered EIs contain usable spatial information.
evidence: This claim is supported by the boundary element model simulations shown in Figure 7.

claim: Chirp-triggered electric images contain usable spatial information.
source: This indicates that chirps consistently alter beats and EIs, at all the different reciprocal positions considered, thus supporting the idea that chirp-triggered EIs contain usable spatial information.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the boundary element model simulations shown in Figure 7.

claim: Brown ghosts spent little time exploring the caged conspecific (12% of the time) and the shelter (14%), while slightly more attention was paid to the novel object (18%), swimming along the walls (ca. 20%) or exploring other objects in the 'open' environment (ca. 35% of the time).
source: We found that on average brown ghosts spent little time exploring the caged conspecific (12% of the time) and the shelter (14%), while slightly more attention was paid to the novel object (18%), swimming along the walls (ca. 20%) or exploring other objects in the 'open' environment (ca. 35% of the time).
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral data from the novel environment exploration assay shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Female brown ghosts spent more time swimming in the open space areas of the arena, as opposed to swimming closer to the tank walls.
source: In particular, female brown ghosts spent more time swimming in the open space areas of the arena, as opposed to swimming closer to the tank walls (thigmotaxis; Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Male behavior showed a different trend as males spent comparatively more time swimming close to the tank walls and more time in contact with conspecifics.
source: Male behavior showed a different trend as males spent comparatively more time swimming close to the tank walls and more time in contact with conspecifics (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Most chirps were produced in close proximity to the caged conspecific.
source: Most chirps were produced in close proximity to the caged conspecific (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the spatial analysis of chirp locations shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Chirps were mostly produced when subjects were located at 30°, 150°, or 330° angles relative to the axis defined by the mesh tube.
source: Analysis of the angles and distances of fish during chirps revealed that first, chirps were mostly produced when subjects were located at 30°, 150°, or 330° angles relative to the axis defined by the mesh tube (Figure 8D)
evidence: This claim is supported by the angular distribution analysis shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Most chirps were produced at a distance of less than 25–50 cm.
source: and second, most chirps were produced at a distance of less than 25–50 cm (Figure 8E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the distance distribution analysis shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Chirps of different types were not all produced at similar angles.
source: Interestingly, chirps of different types were not all produced at similar angles: while type 1 and type 2 chirps seem to be more often produced at 30–150°, type 3 chirps – produced in this experiment only by males – seem to be used in the ±30° range (i.e. on the right side of both the arena and the plane representing the angles).
evidence: This claim is supported by the angular distribution analysis shown in Figure 8D.

claim: All chirp types, except for rises, were produced within a 50 cm radius from the conspecific fish.
source: All chirp types, except for rises, were produced within a 50 cm radius from the conspecific fish (Figure 8E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the distance distribution analysis shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Rises were produced almost ubiquitously, by both sexes, and most of the time at locations far away from the caged fish.
source: Rises were produced almost ubiquitously, by both sexes, and most of the time at locations far away from the caged fish (Appendix 1—figure 11).
evidence: This claim is supported by the spatial analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 11.

claim: Variables associated to beat frequency (such as DF, EOD frequency, sex, chirp type) explain 73.7% of chirp variance.
source: In addition, variables associated to beat frequency (such as DF, EOD frequency, sex, chirp type) explain a good percentage of chirp variance (73.7% of variance explained as opposed to the 55% explained including all other variables 55%; see also Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the factor analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 12.

claim: Most chirps (90%) are produced within a distance corresponding to 1% of the maximum field intensity (i.e. roughly 30 cm).
source: Most chirps (90%) are in fact produced within a distance corresponding to 1% of the maximum field intensity (i.e. roughly 30 cm; Appendix 1—figure 13B), indicating that chirping occurs way above the threshold distance for beat detection (i.e. roughly in the range of 60–120 cm, depending on the study; see appendix 1: Detecting beats at a distance).
evidence: This claim is supported by the electric field modeling shown in Appendix 1—figure 13B.

claim: The total chirp rate increased in absence of light.
source: As expected, the total chirp rate increased in absence of light (Zupanc et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data from the environmental manipulation experiments shown in Figure 9B and a citation to previous research.

claim: The increase in chirp rate was even more pronounced when clutter was present in the environment.
source: More strikingly, the increase was even more pronounced when clutter was present in the environment (Figure 9B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data from the environmental manipulation experiments shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Chirping is significantly affected by the presence of environmental clutter partially disrupting the processing of beat related information during locomotion.
source: Overall, these results indicate that chirping is significantly affected by the presence of environmental clutter partially disrupting – or simply obstructing – the processing of beat related information during locomotion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the environmental manipulation experiments shown in Figure 9.

claim: Chirp rates increased in response to playback signals specifically when they were partially concealed by clutter.
source: We found that chirp rates increased in response to playback signals specifically when they were partially concealed by clutter (Figure 9E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the playback through clutter experiment data shown in Figure 9E.

claim: The most influential factors in chirping are primarily beat frequency (DF) and experience (both environmental and social).
source: Analyzing this data, we found that the most influential factors in chirping are primarily beat frequency (DF) and experience (both environmental and social).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the factor analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Chirp patterns mainly consist of repetitions of the same chirp type which are heavily influenced by DF.
source: Chirp patterns mainly consist of repetitions of the same chirp type which are heavily influenced by DF.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the chirp transition analysis shown in Figure 5 and Appendix 1—figure 3.

claim: Responses to playback chirps inserted into a sinewave stimulus of a particular DF are indistinguishable in terms of chirps emitted by the fish and exploratory behavior (approach/avoidance).
source: Responses to playback chirps inserted into a sinewave stimulus of a particular DF are indistinguishable in terms of chirps emitted by the fish and exploratory behavior (approach/avoidance).
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the playback experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Chirping typically occurs at short ranges, often coinciding with active social approaches.
source: Our behavioral observations of freely swimming fish indicate that chirping typically occurs at short ranges, often coinciding with active social approaches.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the behavioral observations shown in Figure 6 and the novel environment exploration assay shown in Figure 8.

claim: Males chirp considerably more than females.
source: (b) males chirp considerably more than females (Dye, 1987; Bastian et al., 2001; Tallarovic and Zakon, 2002; Dunlap and Larkins-Ford, 2003; Kolodziejski et al., 2007) and are also considerably more aggressive
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: During male interactions (often agonistic) smaller chirps are produced (i.e. shorter duration and lower frequency excursion: type 2) whereas larger chirps (types 1 and 3) are used more often during female-male encounters (presumably courtship-driven).
source: (c) during male interactions (often agonistic) smaller chirps are produced (i.e. shorter duration and lower frequency excursion: type 2) whereas larger chirps (types 1 and 3) are used more often during female-male encounters (presumably courtship-driven)
evidence: This represents the existing hypothesis in the field (communication-hypothesis) that the authors are evaluating.

claim: High chirp rates are observed in mating pairs, with a relatively higher production of large chirps (i.e. type 1 and type 3).
source: (d) high chirp rates are observed in mating pairs, too, with a relatively higher production of large chirps (i.e. type 1 and type 3; Hagedorn and Heiligenberg, 1985; Henninger et al., 2018).
evidence: This represents the existing hypothesis in the field (communication-hypothesis), supported by citations.

claim: Chirps could be used to improve active electrolocation by briefly enhancing beat temporal resolution.
source: Second, chirps could be used to improve active electrolocation by briefly enhancing beat temporal resolution (all types of chirps will increase ELL pyramidal cell firing rates, acting on different input lines; Marsat and Maler, 2010).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors, supported by a citation to research on ELL pyramidal cell responses.

claim: Chirps could be used to enhance electrosensory responses to the beat by enhancing the output of the primary electrosensory afferents or by phase-shifting the carrier EOD.
source: Third, as previously discussed within this study, chirps could be used to enhance electrosensory responses to the beat. This may be achieved by simply enhancing the output of the primary electrosensory afferents (through synchronization of different types of input; Benda et al., 2006) or by phase-shifting the carrier EOD in correspondence of the destructive components of the beat cycles (i.e. the beat minima, as previously suggested by Field et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors, supported by citations to relevant research.

claim: Chirping could be seen as an attempt to adaptively modify the incoming sensory input and maintain optimal contrast levels or a coherent sensory flow, as sniffing does for olfactory perception, whisking and finger movement for tactile sensing, and saccades for vision.
source: In this view, chirping could be seen as an attempt to adaptively modify the incoming sensory input and maintain optimal contrast levels or a coherent sensory flow, as sniffing does for olfactory perception (Hahn et al., 1994), whisking and finger movement for tactile sensing (Krammer et al., 2020) and saccades for vision (Najemnik and Geisler, 2005).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors, drawing an analogy to other sensory systems and supported by citations.

claim: A total of 234 Apteronotus leptorhynchus of both sexes – age ranging between 2 and 3 years – were used in the study.
source: A total of 234 Apteronotus leptorhynchus of both sexes – age ranging between 2 and 3 years – were obtained from tropical fish importers and housed in individual 80x35 x 40 cm aquariums under a 12/12 light cycle.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the animals used in the study.

claim: Fish with a normalized EODf higher than 750 Hz are considered males and those with lower frequencies are considered females.
source: Nevertheless, fish with a normalized EODf higher than 750 Hz are considered males and those with lower frequencies are considered females (Dunlap et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about sex determination, supported by a citation.
